newsitem.title: CHINA: China shows face of ethnic unity after bombings.
newsitem.headline: China shows face of ethnic unity after bombings.

text.p: China's official newspapers on Wednesday splashed pictures of communist leaders together with a popular Moslem singer in a show of ethnic unity after a rash of bombings by Moslem separatists.

The People's Daily, mouthpiece of the ruling Communist Party, ran a front-page picture of Kelimu, a member of the Uighur ethnic minority, his head bowed and clasping the hand of Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin, while Premier Li Peng smiled in the background.

The caption said Kelimu, a member of a government advisory body, wished Jiang well on behalf of the people of Xinjiang, the far western region populated mainly by Moslem Uighurs. China is dominated by Han Chinese.

The Chinese-language Guangming Daily and the English-language China Daily also showed Kelimu together with Jiang. Their picture showed the party chief, wearing a traditional Uighur cap, as he was serenaded at a tea party in Beijing.
The leadership held the party for members of ethnic minorities who hold seats in parliament or its advisory body, the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference.
"The Chinese leadership is trying to put on a show of ethnic unity in the wake of the bomb attacks and rioting," said a Chinese analyst.

Three bombs planted on buses blew up within minutes of each other in Xinjiang's regional capital, Urumqi, on February 25 in an attack apparently coordinated to coincide with funeral rites in Beijing for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping. A fourth bomb failed to explode.

The bomb attacks shattered the image of national unity that China's leadership has sought to project during the delicate transition following Deng's death. Deng died in Beijing on February 19 aged 92.
Exiled Uighur nationalists based in the Kazakh capital of Almaty have claimed responsibility for the bomb attacks.
The nationalists want to set up an independent "East Turkestan" in Xinjiang, home to many Turkic-speaking people, including those of the Uighur minority.
Chinese officials said nine people were killed and 74 injured in the bomb attacks.
A pro-Beijing newspaper quoted Xinjiang's Communist Party chief Wang Lequan as saying seven people had been arrested.
Tomur Dawamat, a Uighur vice-chairman of China's National People's Congress, or parliament, called for unity.
"We will hold higher the banner of patriotism and ethnic equality and unity," the People's Daily quoted Tomur Dawamat as saying.
"(We) are determined to resist plots and activities by hostile forces in the West to use ethnic and religious problems to westernise and divide us," Tomur Dawamat was quoted as saying.

In early February, an anti-Chinese riot erupted in Yining in Xinjiang. Chinese officials said nine people were killed and 198 injured in the riot -- one of the largest, most violent demonstrations for independence in Xinjiang since the 1949 communist takeover.

A bomb blew up on a bus in Beijing last Friday during rush hour, killing at least two people and injuring 30, but Chinese officials say there was no evidence linking the deadly blast with the Urumqi attacks and that no one was killed.
